articles.title: The golden goose
articles.content: IT might be an odd week to write about journalism and indulge in some navel gazing, for much has happened in recent days to keep everyone occupied. From theImran Khan health sagato tragedies that have left most gasping, with thefire at Pimsand themurder of Hina Javed— whose husband has been arrested — in Pindi. And this was just in the twin cities. There was more such news from elsewhere — therape and murder of a child in Haripurand the broader insecurity faced by people living in parts of KP and Balochistan. But it has to be said that the two incidents in Islamabad and Pindi — the power centre of this country — forced the state and society to pay attention. Indeed, at one level, one welcomed the fact that there had been little effort to stop the wall-to-wall coverage of and commentary on these two incidents. After a long time, it seemed as if journalists reported, commented and spoke without looking over their shoulder. So unusual was the experience that it was discussed in more than one newsroom, as insignificant hacks wondered what had happened and why there was some space. After all, now we live in a world where so much of what is happening in the country is a ‘red line’ — from the trees in Islamabad to incidents in our ‘invisible’ provinces to angry protests. Most of it is now left unreported. It is uncovered only by those who are willing to turn into Sherlock Holmes, trawling through social media for ‘events’. Simply the ‘what and when’ is becoming the holy grail. For the television channels beamed into our homes and the newspapers delivered to our phones have learnt that they can only print all the news considered fit to print by the powerful in Pakistan. And this has had an impact on the media industry in ways that are yet to be understood and analysed. Most media owners are no longer interested in investing in human resource. At the most basic level is the credibility gap issue and how it is adding, perhaps, to the shift of people to social media platforms for news. I use the word ‘perhaps’ because it is something I encounter anecdotally. People are moving to social media to learn about the issues no longer covered by the mainstream press. Part of it might be because digital platforms are now providing more innovation in content than the mainstream — for instance, the former now provide space for longer and more meaningful conversations than the same hurried, oft-repeated debate that has become the hallmark of lazy television journalism. Light, satirical commentary on politics is now also more readily available on the newer platforms. But this growth of the social media is now also changing trends within the industry where most acceptable ‘stories’ now make their way to platforms other than the mainstream press. Consider the story about Imran Khan first being taken to hospital for treatment. It came via a vlogger/ journalist on his YouTube show. Similarly, a podcast owned byGeo Newsdisclosed that some IPP parliamentarians are drawing closer to PML-N and might even join it. And even more recently, thenews of Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s possible engagementwas made public in a YouTube conversation before it reached the mainstream. Even before these incidents, the story about Mohammad Zubairmeetingthe then army chief on behalf of Maryam Nawaz and Nawaz Sharif was provided on social media; in hindsight, it seems the news in this case may have been provided by the powers that be. These are some examples of stories which could have been reported by the mainstream media but were not. In some cases, it can be argued the podcasters preferred to use their personal platforms rather than the ones they are employed at. But can it explain all the cases? And it is also noteworthy that employers no longer feel the need to curb their employees on individual platforms. For in an industry where owners no longer care about audiences and are busy making money from government revenue (which is linked to docility rather than journalism), few are interested in either the quality of programmes or of what the anchors are doing outside of the show. Because nothing matters other than sanitised mindless shows and reporting which ensures generous revenue and no official reprimand. This is also why news channels no longer show any of the angst or energy in terms of reporting or content as was the hallmark of the earlier years. Programming has become monotonous; there is little innovation, and field reporting now takes place once there is some push from up above (and I don’t mean the management). Owners are busy counting ad revenue, access and favours and the ones in power are busy patting themselves on the back for having controlled the narrative. And if the people are no longer buying it, the echo chamber doesn’t let anyone find out. But there is an even more serious angle to this. Most media owners are no longer interested in investing in human resource for it is no longer needed as such. Who needs reporters, when reporting simply creates problems? Why bother hiring senior editorial people when stories no longer need to be vetted? And none of this affects the bottom line? Because content and reporting has little to do with how much money can be made. This is why nearly every other day comes the news of one channel or another firing people. It’s not random and neither is it whimsical. It reflects the priorities of an industry whose economic model is not linked to the quality of its output. Soon the industry might be tempted to replace news and programme hosts with AI-generated ones, if the latter come cheap enough and can be controlled. But I wonder if anyone has bothered to think about a day when the media loses its nuisance value entirely. Will the moolah still continue to flow into the coffers of the mainstream? Or will it simply fade into oblivion?
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: The Hindu right in trouble
articles.content: HAVING prospered abroad as an unbridled organisation flaunting different names and profiles for decades, the RSS seems to be in trouble in western cities and townships where unusual rage is surfacing at its documented hatred of Muslims and Christians. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to the US and Canada has come at a fraught time in the organisation’s global and domestic trajectory. The timing of this change in attitude coincides with ayouth movementquestioning the ideological fundamentals of the Modi government at home and decline of Israel as a morally tenable entity in the comity of nations. Israel’s fondness for India’s right-wing Hindu establishment has collaterally damaged India’s reputation as an old comrade in much of Asia, Africa and Latin America. Not quite flattering also is the reality ofPakistan’s rise as a widely wooed global partnerwith India painting itself into a diplomatic corner. When a frustrated Donald Trumpyelled at Israelfor becoming friendless and hated by everyone, Benjamin Netanyahu smiled back, saying he still had India for a friend. The backhanded compliment isn’t lost on the world at large. Where Pakistan is headed, India once claimed the high ground — the reliable friend ready to help untangle strategic and diplomatic knots world leaders needed to fix urgently. There was a time when leaders sought out India to intervene as an honest broker to wind down the traumatic Korean conflict, and they remained grateful that Nehru stepped in. There was a time when Indira Gandhi was urged by the Non-Aligned Movement to broker peace in the lacerating Iran-Iraq war. She dispatched senior diplomat Romesh Bhandari to placate the warring arch-foes as only a trusted Indian envoy could. And though the war eventually ended when a US warship shot down an Iranian Airbus packed with Dubai shoppers, India’s helping hand continued to be valued in the entire region. Today, the world may be interested in India’s lucrative market, but sans the respect India once commanded. There were Indian stowaways slinking out abroad even then, but they were never repatriated in handcuffs and fetters as Trump did with Indian citizens recently, even though Narendra Modi had canvassed support for his re-election in 2020. The RSS prides itself as a shadowy unregistered paramilitary body, whereas even the Nazis were a registered party. The RSS prides itself as a shadowy unregistered paramilitary body, whereas even the Nazis were a registered party. Critics point to its opaque financial resources at home and abroad. Those resources may have come under a cloud on two fronts. The opposition in India is demanding the group’s registration amid calls for transparency, which the RSS is assiduously resisting. Abroad, Trump hasincreased the visa feeto impossible figures for IT professionals to seek, and IT professionals are known to be the mainstay of RSS sympathisers and its finances in the US. How has the RSS stayed popular among the Indian diaspora was a question that a huge number of protesters in the US and Canada were asking ahead of and during Bhagwat’s visit. It rode piggyback with the powerful Israel lobby. But Christian Zionists and Jewish Zionists are under attack from within the Democratic and Republican establishments with Zohran Mamdani and Tucker Carlson being the tip of the iceberg. The consequent decline of Israel’s prowess is not good news for the RSS. Bhagwat’s reportedly conciliatory tone during his New York meeting presaged a looming crisis for the group in its various avatars. At the public meeting, he claimed that Hindus who wish to see Muslims out of India would cease to be Hindus if they did so. The comments were borrowed from a brainstorming meeting he organised in Delhi in 2018. Did that stop the bloodcurdling assaults on Muslims and Christians or the Dalits from Hindutva zealots? No. Even as Bhagwat was in New York or preparing to get there, the ground reality in India defied his claims. Anew law in Maharashtrawas being unveiled for Christians visiting the church to fill out a form to say they were not being coerced to convert. Is there a similar law for those forced or lured to convert to Hinduism? Around then the decks were also being cleared to free the Hindutva fanatic from jail who had burnt alive the Australian priest and caregiver Graham Steines and his two sons in their jeep in 1990. Two faux Hindu gurus jailed for rape, with one sentenced also for murder, are enjoying paroles and furloughs at will, while intellectual dissenters like Umar Khalid are languishing in prison, with no sign of a trial starting soon. Nehru used to say that the RSS was not a trustworthy organisation. Its leaders said one thing and did another. For example, the RSS distanced itself from Gandhi’s killer Godse but distributed sweets at the assassination, according to Sardar Patel. Modi, an RSS man did one better. He freed Samjhauta Express terror bomb accused Sadhvi Pragya from jail, made her an MP and then watched her praising Godse as a hero for killing Gandhi. Bhagwat reportedly told the Delhi brainstorming that some parts of former RSS chief Golwalkar’s book needed to be discarded. Let’s check it out. In Chapter V of his bookWe or Our Nationhood Defined, Golwalkar says: “The non-Hindu peoples in Hindustan must either adopt the Hindu culture and language, must learn to respect and hold in reverence Hindu religion, must entertain no idea but those of the glorification of the Hindu race and culture, ie, of the Hindu nation and must lose their separate existence to merge in the Hindu race, or may stay in the country, wholly subordinated to the Hindu Nation, claiming nothing, deserving no privileges, far less any preferential treatment — not even citizen’s rights.” What else is being pursued over the last 12-plus years? If Bhagwat is trying to rewrite the Golwalkar book, it indicates two possibilities. One, the RSS has gone fundamentally at loggerheads with the Modi government. Two, the RSS is in serious trouble. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Peaceful path
articles.content: WHAT have peaceful democracy protests achieved in our long autocratic history? A look at those against Gen Ayub, Zia and Musharraf, and the murkier 1977 protests, offers clues. Political and economic exclusion and repression fuel protests. A shocking abuse, disputed polls, power grab or economic pain often provides the spark. Movement traits (coalition size, muscle, leadership and tactics) and context (urban density, external aid etc.) provide circuitry for the fire to spread. Regime cohesion, repression and foreign help provide the fire brigade. But even if they win a battle, they may lose the war if allies lack the strength and a democratic agenda. Exclusion and repression fuelled all four. Economic pain added fuel in 1969 and 1977. Three targeted outright autocrats; the 1977 a more legitimate civilian. A student’s killing under Ayub Khan, poll disputes under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Pervez Musharraf’s firing of the chief justice were sparks. The 1983 protest lacked a clear spark, so it stoked a smaller fire despite the fact that repression was at its peak. Context decided no one’s fate, ties with the US were strained under Bhutto in 1977 and strong under Zia in 1983. Movement traits varied. All were coalitions with varied social bases. The 1969 one was mainly a leftist student-worker-political one. The 1977 protest mainly rallied conservative parties, traders and clergy. The 1983 protest united the PPP, its 1977 foes and progressive groups. The 2007 demonstrations drew in centrist lawyers, parties and activists. But the social base or ideology always counted less than the size of the coalition. Major politicians led more in 1969 and 1977 than in 1983 and 2007. Without a democratic agenda, political allies can lose the battle. Tactics differed too. All had shutdowns, but 1969 had more worker strikes, 1977 business closures, 1983 civil disobedience and 2007 court boycotts and marches. But unlike some global protests where mammoth crowds paralysed capitals to topple regimes in days, all four were smaller, spread across cities and unfolded slowly. So, regime strength was decisive. The US cut support to Ayub in 1965. The army did so in 1969 after 10 years as his health failed, letting the fire raze the autocrat’s fort. Bhutto too alienated the military, which ousted him; Zia survived via a cohesive military and coercive capacity in 1983. Musharraf slowly lost US and military support. So, fractured fire brigades let small crowds win three times. But the autocratic base always survived to reverse even small gains. In 1969, a general took over to hold our first fair polls but rejected their result, leading to tragedy. Bhutto gained power but ruled harshly. The 2007-09 gains yielded the most fruits: freer polls, freedoms and good laws. But most gains were ironically reversed with help from their architect parties. So, the main legacy of decades of struggles is the badly mauled 1973 Constitution. This reflects autocracy’s strengths: institutional cohesion, strong control and surveillance, a business empire to reward allies, and hold over the piety, propriety and patriotism mantra. Coalitions broke soon, while political leaders, often veterans of past autocracies, ruled harshly. Our failures mirror global ones. Our review suggests only about 40 per cent of successful postwar peaceful protests outside Europe led to durable democracy. Most had strong pro-democracy parties and iconic democrats like Nelson Mandela. But peaceful protests rarely defeat a cohesive autocratic establishment; they usually succeed when the autocratic base itself lets an autocrat fall. Armed struggles do worse: only 26pc after 1900 won, and just 6pc led to democracy. They may topple decaying orders but often build a new autocracy later. Neither can defeat a strong autocracy. But there is a third way: constitutional change often backed by grassroots work that slowly ends auto-cracy. Repression today provides ample fuel; disputed polls, power grabs, economic pain, abuses and judicial curbs have given many sparks. Yet no fire has spread. The missing circuitry is a coalition able to integrate local anger into national action. This reflects regime tactics based on past lessons — arrests, speech bans and co-optation of civil society — plus the impact of past curbs on student and worker groups. But anger against repression is like dammed floodwater that finds new outlets to cause havoc. The current hybrid set-up may face the same fate, leaving us for the umpteenth time to rebuild democracy from autocracy’s wreckage. However, durable democracy will require politicians to commit to democratic norms and grassroots work. The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experiences across 50 countries.
articles.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza

articles.title: Closing the gap
articles.content: WHEN a child is reported stunted, it is tempting to ask which ministry is responsible. Is it the ministry of health, nutrition, social protection, or others? In reality, all of them are responsible institutionally — and none when it comes to implementation on the ground. Forty per cent of Pakistan’s children under five years are stunted while 17.7pc suffer from wasting, as of 2018. The scale of this crisis cannot be understated. Driven by more than just diet, the onset of stunting in a child is driven cumulatively by maternal nutrition, household poverty, food security, sanitation, healthcare, and education. Over the past several years and despite frequent administrative changes, Pakistan has actively recognised this reality, progressively building a multi-sectoral policy architecture to tackle stunting at both federal and provincial levels. However, progress has remained limited. The challenge the country faces today is not a shortage of programming: it is a recurrent gap between high-level multisectoral policy and local-level multisectoral delivery. While health and nutrition were devolved to provinces following the 18th Amendment, parallel ministries and a persistent federal-provincial overlap have stymied how national-level targets trickle down to the local level. With the 2018 National Nutrition Survey revealing steep geographical disparities in stunting that would otherwise remain concealed behind national-level averages, responsible institutions are forced to ask an important question: after targets are set, how do we reach the last mile of multisectoral coordination and delivery? Pakistan’s stunting problem needs more than a nutrition response. Pakistan’s social protection system offers one promising avenue through the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP). The programme’s latest independent evaluation in May 2026 painted a promising picture: child beneficiaries displayed an 18pc lower risk of stunting at 12 months, a 12pc reduction in child anaemia, and a 17pc increase in full immunisation coverage. At the same time, the evaluation offered a warning — and an opportunity — that runs the risk of being ignored: despite improved pregnancy weight gain, fewer than 25pc of participating women achieved adequate dietary diversity. That is because despite the BNP’s nutrition-specific interventions, multisectoral factors continue to affect maternal malnutrition and, ultimately, child stunting. A cash transfer cannot secure nutritious foods if they are not available in local markets. A health facility cannot compensate for sanitation. And, a nutrition programme cannot improve the socioeconomic conditions shaping what families eat on a daily basis. We already have evidence that the programme’s delivery systems work. The opportunity now lies in using what the programme already has — its reach into vulnerable households, service delivery network, and growing data infrastructure — to connect those households to other government sectoral programmes at the local level. BNP operates across 158 districts on one of the country’s most extensive social protection datasets to date. The National Socio-economic Registry already provides a mechanism for identifying and reaching vulnerable households, while BNP tracks additional maternal and child health data. These datasets can be used to diagnostically identify districts where BNP households show particularly high concentrations of specific risk factors. Are households lacking safe water? Are mothers receiving antenatal and postnatal care? Are children immunised? Are girls attending schools? Can families afford robust diets? The answers would determine which government departments would need to act next in addressing stunting locally. Figuring out the accountability and ownership piece is the next step — Indonesia offers a useful model. Under its Stranas Stunting convergence strategy, districts analyse local stunting and service gaps, use those findings to align existing departmental plans and budgets, and then monitor whether priority households receive the services they need. Cross-sectoral convergence for stunting is often misunderstood as a plurality of programmes. In reality, the principle is simpler: convergence occurs when government programmes target the same problem, in the same place, for the same child. The early successes of BNP offer an opportunity for Pakistan to not simply scale social protection and cash transfer programmes by expanding the number of beneficiaries reached, but to connect its investments in child and maternal health, WASH, food systems, education, and population to existing platforms that already reach vulnerable households. The writer is an analyst working for an international organisation that provides counsel for effective social impact.
articles.author: Shizah Kashif

articles.title: A reckoning
articles.content: LAST week’shorrific fire tragedy at the Pims’ nurseryhas elicited a flurry of responses from the state. Inquiries have been launched,officials have faced the axe, and pledges have been made to rectify the glaring lacunae that led to the heart-wrenching deaths of 14 newborns at the Islamabad hospital. Yet while the sudden burst of activity is expected, these promises will remain meaningless unless the state prioritises safety protocols at hospitals and all major public and private buildings. The findings of the inquiry report are damning. It says that while the cause of the fire cannot be conclusively established at this point, there were “serious shortcomings” in Pims’ fire safety arrangements. A fire had also broken out at the same hospital in July. However, after that blaze, “corrective measures had not been adequately implemented”. Those responsible for such criminal negligence must be made to answer for their lapses. Elsewhere, the Islamabad administration hasswung into action, sealing buildings and fining hospitals for fire safety violations. Meanwhile, in Rawalpindi, it has emerged that there are no hydrants at any government hospital in the entire division. The Punjab government, on the other hand, hasannouncedseveral steps to prevent similar tragedies. This includes deploying Rescue 1122 units at all teaching hospitals in the province, as well as preparing SOPs for nurseries and neonatology units. These are positive first steps, and they need to be made part of established procedures nationwide to prevent future tragedies. The Sindh government has alsoidentifiedover 3,300 buildings for safety audits. The provincial chapter of the Pakistan Medical Association has warned that many health facilities in Sindh remain vulnerable, particularly rural and district hospitals. It has also called for third-party safety and security audits of all public and private hospitals in the province. These warnings must be heeded before another tragedy occurs. What must emerge from all of this is a resolve to put safety first, especially in settings like hospitals, schools, factories, apartments and other buildings where large numbers of people live and work. The outrage must be channelled into proactive public policy where the safety of citizens is prioritised. There have been many such tragic episodes in recent memory — theBaldia fire disaster,Gul Plazaetc. However, in the aftermath of the Pims blaze, it cannot be business as usual. Accidents happen, but if established safety protocols are in place, precious lives can be saved and the damage minimised. Clearly, these protocols were not in place at the Pims’ nursery. In most Pakistani cities, fire hazards sit in plain sight. Addressing these dangers is a monumental task, but we cannot afford to sacrifice more lives to official lethargy.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: EV transition
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S transition to electric mobility is stalling not for want of ambition but consistency. The government’s plan for 30pc EV penetration within five years, meant to save $4.5bn annually on fuel imports, sits uneasily alongside a policy environment that sends mixed signals to investors, manufacturers, auto parts makers and consumers alike. Oil marketing companies, which should be natural partners in building the charging infrastructure needed, keep pouring capital into conventional retail expansion. The absence of investment in charging infrastructure reflects where OMCs expect the money to keep flowing. Their decision is shaped directly by what government policy signals, or does not signal, about the future. With different lobbies trying to influence the upcoming auto policy, the government has delayed its announcement, creating more market uncertainty. The situation is not unique to Pakistan, but our history of policy reversals gives such lobbying particular traction. Consumers remember. Investors remember. This is one of the biggest obstacles to EV adoption: nobody wants to bet on infrastructure or vehicle purchases when the policy underpinning them could be reversed many times in its five-year life. The way out is not to pick winners indefinitely but to be clear about which winner is being picked, and for how long. Electric mobility deserves front-loaded fiscal support: import duty concessions on batteries and EV components, purchase incentives for consumers, and preferential tax treatment that make the total cost of ownership competitive with conventional ICE and hybrid technologies. But even incentives for EVs should have a sunset date and be linked to the manufacturers’ localisation effort. This is standard practice in every successful EV market. Beyond that specific push for electrification, policy should stop playing referee between technologies. Whatever comes next should compete on its own economic and environmental merit rather than on whoever has the better lobbyist in Islamabad. A technology-neutral framework beyond the EV push would strip entrenched players of their lobbying incentive, letting markets decide which non-EV technologies survive. Charging infrastructure will follow this transition, not lead it. OMCs will not sink capital into charging networks ahead of demand — that misreads how the industry allocates money. Push EV sales past a threshold, and charging becomes commercially rational on its own.
articles.author: Editorial
